title: Nadolol and placebo comparison study in the prophylactic treatment of migraine.
journal: The Journal of the American Osteopathic Association

screening.rationale: Title indicates a randomized nadolol versus placebo trial for migraine prophylaxis but no abstract or full text was available to determine whether the paper analyzed placebo/nocebo effects rather than using placebo solely as an efficacy comparator.

classification.summary: No abstract available; reported a randomized controlled trial comparing nadolol versus placebo for migraine prophylaxis in adults.

title: Placebo effect in tinnitus management.
journal: Otolaryngology--head and neck surgery : official journal of American Academy of Otolaryngology-Head and Neck Surgery
abstract: Masking devices, lidocaine, and analog oral forms of lidocaine have all been reported as being effective forms of therapy to relieve tinnitus. Many studies, however, have used single-blind protocols and were possibly biased by placebo effects. To investigate the contributions of a placebo effect in clinical tinnitus studies, 25 tinnitus patients who had received a placebo injection in a previous double-blind lidocaine study were contacted on the pretense that they would receive a test dose of lidocaine; the 20 who responded were included in this study. A 5 cc bolus of placebo saline solution instead of lidocaine was then administered to each patient. Forty percent of the patients reported a change in their tinnitus following the placebo injection. The results of this study serve to point out the inherent flaws in straight clinical trials, and that the success rates achieved in such uncontrolled clinical investigations may be biased by the placebo effects.

screening.rationale: Empirical study that explicitly investigated placebo-induced change in tinnitus by administering a saline injection under the pretense of lidocaine, thus analyzing placebo response/effect.

classification.summary: Contacted prior trial participants and administered a saline injection presented as lidocaine; 40% reported change in tinnitus, highlighting placebo contributions in tinnitus trials.
classification.key_finding: 40% of 20 participants reported a change in tinnitus after a saline placebo injection given under the pretense of lidocaine.

title: Physiological reactivity to alcohol cues and the awareness of an alcohol effect in a double-blind placebo design.

screening.rationale: Title indicates a double-blind placebo design studying physiological and awareness responses to alcohol cues, making placebo effects/responses the apparent object of study.

classification.summary: Examined physiological reactivity to alcohol cues and subjective awareness of alcohol effects using a double-blind placebo beverage design.

title: Ethics. A perspective on the proper use of placebos in research and therapy.

screening.rationale: Title indicates a perspective on ethical use of placebos in research and therapy, making placebo ethics the main subject despite no abstract.

classification.summary: Discusses ethical considerations and guidance for appropriate use of placebos in research and clinical therapy.

title: Erythrapheresis compared with placebo apheresis in patients with polycythaemia secondary to hypoxic lung disease.
abstract: We have assessed the effects of erythrapheresis, a method of isovolaemic haemodilution, and placebo apheresis in 10 patients with polycythaemia secondary to chronic hypoxic lung disease (Mean PaO2 7.2kPa (54 mm Hg]. The mean packed cell volume decreased from 0.60 to 0.48, with significant decreases in blood viscosity at both high and low shear rates (p less than 0.001). The 6-min walking distance improved after erythrapheresis with no significant placebo effect of the procedure compared to control subjects (p less than 0.01). Erythrapheresis is a safe procedure for packed cell volume reduction. It is associated with clinical improvement and there is no demonstrable placebo effect on exercise tolerance.

screening.rationale: Randomized controlled trial used a placebo apheresis (sham) arm and reported on absence of a placebo effect for exercise tolerance, so placebo effect was an object of study.

classification.summary: Compared erythrapheresis versus placebo (sham) apheresis in 10 patients with secondary polycythaemia due to hypoxic lung disease and found erythrapheresis reduced hematocrit and improved 6-min walk distance, with no demonstrable placebo effect on exercise tolerance.
classification.key_finding: Erythrapheresis reduced packed cell volume (0.60 to 0.48) and improved 6-min walk (p<0.01); placebo apheresis produced no significant improvement in exercise tolerance.

title: Transdermal therapeutic system scopolamine (TTSS), dimenhydrinate, and placebo--a comparative study at sea.
abstract: The efficacy of transdermally administered scopolamine was compared with the efficacy of oral dimenhydrinate and placebo therapy in the prevention of motion sickness at sea. Medication was administered on a controlled double blind basis to 140 subjects. A placebo effect reduced the motion sickness incidence (MSI) from 57.69% in the control group to 43.47%. Administration of dimenhydrinate reduced the MSI to 22.22% and the use of Transdermal Therapeutic System Scopolamine (TTSS) further reduced the MSI to 16.66%. TTSS afforded 61.67% protection against motion sickness at sea, compared to 48.88% protection with dimenhydrinate.

screening.rationale: Randomized double-blind trial that reported and quantified a placebo effect (placebo vs control) on motion sickness incidence, so placebo response/effect was an object of study.

classification.summary: Compared transdermal scopolamine, oral dimenhydrinate, and placebo in 140 adults at sea and reported that placebo reduced motion sickness incidence versus control and that active treatments reduced it further.
classification.key_finding: Placebo reduced motion sickness incidence from 57.69% (control) to 43.47%; dimenhydrinate to 22.22% and TTSS to 16.66% (TTSS ~61.7% protection).

title: "Natural history" of Crohn's disease. An analytic review of the placebo lesson.

screening.rationale: Title indicates an analytic review focused on the placebo 'lesson' in Crohn's disease trials, meeting inclusion for placebo science/response analysis despite no abstract.

classification.summary: Reviewed placebo lessons and natural history in Crohn's disease trials, focusing on placebo/remission rates and trial methodology.

title: The influence of mechanical vibratory stimulation and transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation on experimental pruritus induced by histamine.
abstract: The effect of conditioning mechanical vibratory stimulation and transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS) on experimentally induced pruritus was studied on 12 healthy subjects. Pruritus was provoked by intradermal injection of histamine on the upper arm. Vibration at 10, 100 and 200 Hz and TENS at 2 and 100 Hz were applied (i) over or (ii) proximal (in the same dermatome) to the pruritic area for a period of 5 min following itch elicitation. In addition the influence of a 5 min pre-stimulatory regimen of the injection area was investigated (iii). The results obtained were compared with unconditioned values and with those obtained following a placebo conditioning procedure (i, ii). It was found that vibratory as well as electrical stimulation, for all frequencies used, reduced subjective itch intensity. Vibration at 100 Hz was the most effective mode of stimulation especially when applied directly to the pruritic area. Conditioning with 100 Hz vibration was also the most effective mode for reducing the duration of the itch response as well as the total experience of pruritus (estimated as a total itch index). Induction time to partial and maximal itch alleviation was shortest for 100 Hz vibration. The results indicate that treatment of pruritic conditions with conditioning stimulation, especially vibration, may be of therapeutic interest.

screening.rationale: Experimental human study manipulated conditioning/vibratory and TENS stimulation versus unconditioned and placebo conditioning controls to test effects on histamine-induced itch, meeting the placebo-effect/conditioning inclusion criterion.

classification.summary: Tested vibration and TENS conditioning in 12 healthy adults with histamine-induced itch and found 100 Hz vibration most effectively reduced subjective itch intensity, duration, and total itch index versus unconditioned and placebo conditioning.
classification.key_finding: Vibration at 100 Hz produced the largest and fastest reduction in subjective itch compared with other frequencies, TENS, unconditioned and placebo conditioning.

title: Effects of alcohol and expectancies on verbal aggression in men and women.

screening.rationale: No abstract or full text provided; title indicates alcohol expectancies were manipulated but it's unclear whether the study used a placebo/expectancy design isolating placebo/nocebo effects or focused on alcohol pharmacology.

classification.summary: Study examined effects of alcohol and expectancies on verbal aggression in men and women; abstract not available so methods and focus on placebo/expectancy designs could not be confirmed.

title: Placebo effect in surgery for Meniere's disease: a three-year follow-up study of patients in a double blind placebo controlled study on endolymphatic sac shunt surgery.
abstract: In a previously published double blind, placebo controlled study, the efficacy of an endolymphatic sac-mastoid shunt was compared with a purely placebo operation (mastoidectomy) in controlling the symptoms in 30 patients with typical Meniere's disease. Minor differences could be demonstrated after one year between patients with the shunt versus the sham operation, but the greatest difference was between the pre- and postoperative scores, and both groups improved significantly. It was concluded that the impact of the various endolymphatic sac shunts upon the symptoms in patients with Meniere's disease is highly unspecific, and that the 70% improvement in both our groups was most likely caused by a placebo effect. The patients have now been regularly followed for a minimum of 3 years and the symptoms registered whenever present. The results of hearing tests, the patients' own evaluation, and the investigator's evaluation (while still unaware of the type of operation in each patient) show that the 3-year results are the same as our results from the first year: no significant difference could be found between the two groups.

screening.rationale: Randomized double-blind sham-surgery trial that explicitly analyzed improvement in both shunt and placebo-operation groups and attributed it to a placebo effect.

classification.summary: Followed 30 Meniere's disease patients randomized to endolymphatic sac shunt versus sham mastoidectomy for three years and found both groups improved (~70%) with no significant difference between groups, interpreted as a placebo effect.
classification.key_finding: About 70% improvement in both shunt and sham groups at one and three years with no between-group difference, suggesting improvement was nonspecific/placebo-related.

title: Placebo--the universal drug.

screening.rationale: No abstract or full text provided; title implies a broad discussion of placebo but available text is insufficient to confirm that placebo/nocebo is the main subject and the article type.

classification.summary: Presents a broad discussion of the placebo concept and its clinical and physiological relevance, based on title and MeSH terms (no abstract available).

title: Occlusal splints (MORA) vs. placebos show no difference in strength in symptomatic subjects: double blind/cross-over study.
journal: Canadian journal of applied sport sciences. Journal canadien des sciences appliquees au sport
abstract: Many athletes with or without occlusal problems are now using mandibular orthopedic repositioning appliances (MORA) or simply occlusal splints, supposedly to enhance skeletal muscle strength. Recent research to establish these claims has suffered from design inaccuracies. In theory, the MORA reduces temporomandibular stress during clenched jaw efforts. It is suggested that pain in the temporomandibular joint (TMJ) and surrounding musculature could limit a maximum effort during an athletic endeavour. Eight subjects with TMJ disorders were tested for strength changes in 4 muscle groups with a custom MORA and placebo splint in a tightly controlled double-blind cross-over protocol using a Cybex II dynamometer. A two-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) did not show significant differences in strength change between the two splints. Neither were there any trends that would suggest strength benefits from the MORA.

screening.rationale: Double-blind crossover trial explicitly compared an active occlusal splint (MORA) with a placebo splint to test causal effects on muscle strength.

classification.summary: Tested strength in eight TMJ-disorder subjects in a double-blind crossover comparing custom MORA versus placebo splint and found no significant strength differences.
classification.key_finding: No significant difference in muscle strength between MORA and placebo splints (two-way ANOVA, n=8).

title: Expectancy effects on anxiety and self-generated cognitive strategies in high and low dental-anxious females.
journal: Journal of behavior therapy and experimental psychiatry
abstract: Expectancy effects on self-reported anxiety and self-generated cognitive strategies were evaluated in a dental analogue by means of a film response questionnaire and an interview. Seventy-two female college subjects, half high and half low in self-reported dental fear were assigned to three levels of expectancy set (positive, fearful and neutral) induced by means of a slide presentation and verbal set. Although expectancy effects on post-film anxiety were not significant, differences due to dental fear level were found. Interview protocols were rated for general cognitive response style (coping, catastrophizing or no strategy), arousal and absorption. Discriminant function analysis between response styles indicated that arousal level provided a strong contribution to the discriminant functions differentiating between the general response styles, separating non-strategy users from catastrophizers. Specific ratings of reported absorption were related to whether or not cognitive coping strategies were used. Expectancy set was related to the direction of these cognitions. The findings validate the use of dental analogue studies for investigating dental fear.

screening.rationale: Experimental manipulation of expectancy (positive, fearful, neutral) and analysis of its effects on self-reported anxiety and cognitive strategies fits inclusion for expectation/placebo-context effects.

classification.summary: Assigned college women to positive, fearful, or neutral expectancy sets and measured dental-analogue anxiety and cognitive coping, finding no significant expectancy effect on post-film anxiety but expectancy influenced direction of self-generated cognitions.
classification.key_finding: Expectancy condition did not significantly change self-reported post-film anxiety, but it was related to the direction of cognitive responses (coping vs catastrophizing) and interacted with baseline dental fear level.

title: Antihypertensive effect of enalapril as first-step treatment of mild and moderate uncomplicated essential hypertension. Evaluation by two methods of blood pressure measurement.
abstract: The new angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitor enalapril (MK-421), was given in a single daily dose of 20 mg to 53 patients with uncomplicated essential hypertension. Its effects were compared with those of a placebo given to 47 patients on a double-blind randomized basis. The blood pressure was measured in all patients by a physician, using a mercury sphygmomanometer, and by an automatic device in the absence of the physician. After 15 days of treatment, enalapril induced a significant reduction in systolic blood pressure (161.4 +/- 13 versus 145.1 +/- 15, p less than 0.001) and in diastolic blood pressure (103.3 +/- 6 versus 92.9 +/- 8, p less than 0.001) measured by the physician. The magnitude of the fall in blood pressure was identical after 30 days of active treatment. The reduction in blood pressure induced by enalapril was similarly detected by both methods of measurement, despite the fact that blood pressure values were higher when measured by the physician. A placebo effect was observed with the physician's values that was not present with the automatically recorded values. A very significant correlation between blood pressure values obtained by these two methods was observed. However, among nine of 53 patients treated with enalapril, a difference in the decrease of blood pressure of 10 mm Hg or more was noted between the two methods of measurement. The decrease in blood pressure occurred with no change noted in the pulse rate or orthostatic hypotension. Plasma renin activity increased after treatment. No changes were observed in creatinine clearance and plasma electrolyte levels.

screening.rationale: Although primarily an antihypertensive RCT, the paper reported and analyzed a placebo effect (physician-measured BP showed a placebo response absent in automatic measures), meeting inclusion criterion for placebo/nocebo analysis.

classification.summary: Randomized double-blind trial of enalapril versus placebo in mild-to-moderate hypertension found drug-induced BP reductions and a placebo-associated BP fall on physician-measured values that was absent on automatic recordings.
classification.key_finding: Observed a significant placebo effect on physician-measured blood pressure but not on automatic device measurements (N=100).

title: Placebo treatment of polymorphous light sensitivity.

screening.rationale: No abstract or methods available; title indicates placebo treatment of polymorphous light sensitivity but insufficient information to confirm that the paper studied placebo/nocebo effects or responses.

classification.summary: No abstract available; title indicated a placebo treatment was used for polymorphous light sensitivity, but methods, design, and outcomes were not reported in the available record.

title: Psychotherapy: the powerful placebo.
journal: Journal of consulting and clinical psychology

screening.rationale: Title indicates the paper is a conceptual/theoretical piece arguing that psychotherapy operates as a placebo, so placebo science is the main subject despite no abstract.

classification.summary: Argued that psychotherapy operates largely as a powerful placebo and discussed implications for research and clinical practice.

title: Physician beliefs, attitudes, and prescribing behavior for anti-inflammatory drugs.
abstract: Psychologists have distinguished between "beliefs" and "attitudes" to help explain human behavior. To investigate the relationship between physician beliefs, attitudes, and their prescribing behavior for anti-inflammatory medication, 30 doctors in two Veterans Administration clinics were surveyed by questionnaire, and 1,265 of their prescriptions were collected. Their estimates of drug costs and the percent of patients who would have response to therapy or side effects were considered "beliefs." The "attitudes" measured were the relative importance physicians placed on six factors when choosing therapy: effectiveness, side effects, likelihood of compliance, placebo effect, cost, and the patient's perception of the physician. Physicians believed that efficacy of the different proprietary nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory agents and aspirin compounds was comparable. They perceived indomethacin as more toxic than other nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (p less than 0.01), and enteric-coated aspirin as less toxic than plain aspirin (p less than 0.01). Physicians wrote 5.7 times as many prescriptions for proprietary nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory agents as for aspirin compounds. A correlation was not observed between relative use of proprietary agents versus aspirin compounds and beliefs about costs, response rates, or side effects rates; however, attitudes regarding the importance of cost and placebo effects were correlated with prescribing behavior (p less than 0.05).

screening.rationale: Survey study of physicians' attitudes explicitly measured the perceived importance of the placebo effect and related prescribing behavior, qualifying as placebo-science (attitudes/clinical use).

classification.summary: Surveyed 30 VA physicians about beliefs and attitudes toward NSAIDs/aspirin and collected 1,265 prescriptions, finding attitudes about cost and placebo effects correlated with prescribing patterns.
classification.key_finding: Attitudes regarding the importance of cost and placebo effects were correlated with greater use of proprietary NSAIDs versus aspirin (p < 0.05).

title: Schizophrenia, hemodialysis, and the placebo effect. Results and issues.
abstract: This report presents the results of a double-blind study that examines the impact of hemodialysis on patients with chronic schizophrenia. Twelve patients were randomly assigned to sham and 12 patients to active dialysis. All patients experienced a drug washout period and were then followed up over an eight-week period. A statistically significant condition by weeks interaction was found, with patients in the sham group improving and patients in the active dialysis group decompensating over the last weeks of the trial. This complex finding fails to support the hypothesized efficacy of hemodialysis in the treatment of schizophrenia but also fails to support a simple placebo explanation for positive results reported in earlier open studies. The methodologic complications are reviewed, and a possible direction for future research is presented.

screening.rationale: Randomized double-blind sham vs active dialysis trial reported improvement in the sham group and discussed placebo explanations, so the sham/placebo response is an object of analysis.

classification.summary: Reported a double-blind randomized trial (n=24) comparing sham versus active hemodialysis in chronic schizophrenia and found sham patients improved while active patients decompensated, discussing methodological implications for placebo explanations.
classification.key_finding: Sham (placebo) dialysis group showed improvement over eight weeks while active dialysis patients worsened, challenging simple efficacy or placebo explanations.

title: Psychopharmacologic validation of atypical depression.
abstract: Sixty patients meeting specific criteria for atypical depression completed 6 weeks of double-blind, randomly assigned treatment with phenelzine, imipramine, or placebo. Patients who had a history of spontaneous panic attacks or hysteriod dysphoric features showed extremely low placebo-response rates, moderate responses to imipramine, and high rates of response to phenelzine. Conversely, patients without such features responded moderately well to all three treatments. Based on preliminary data, MAOI-specific atypical depression does appear to exist, although in more delimited forms than previously recognized.

screening.rationale: Randomized double-blind trial that reported and compared placebo-response rates across clinical subgroups, making placebo response an object of analysis.

classification.summary: Randomized double-blind trial of phenelzine, imipramine, and placebo in 60 patients with atypical depression that reported differing placebo-response rates across clinical subgroups.
classification.key_finding: Found low placebo-response rates in patients with panic or hysteriod dysphoric features and moderate-to-high placebo responses in patients without those features.

title: Understanding placebos in dentistry.
journal: Journal of the American Dental Association (1939)
abstract: The placebo effect is capable of relieving pain and affective disorders. The mechanism of placebo action is pharmacologic and psychologic, being related to the patient-practitioner relationship and the clinical treatment setting. The placebo effect also occurs with all active or real treatments. The effects of placebos in management of orofacial pain and MPD syndrome have been demonstrated. Placebo effects may account for a third to two-thirds of responses in mandibular dysfunction. Many treatments suggested for management of pain may be acting solely as placebos. Health professionals active in management of pain should understand and use the placebo effect to improve patient care.

screening.rationale: Narrative review whose main subject was placebo effects in orofacial/dental pain and their mechanisms and clinical use, meeting the 'placebo science' inclusion criteria.

classification.summary: Reviews evidence that placebo effects are substantial in orofacial and mandibular dysfunction pain and recommends clinicians understand and use placebo mechanisms to improve care.
classification.key_finding: Estimated that one-third to two-thirds of responses in mandibular dysfunction may be attributable to placebo effects.

title: The effects of role preparation for psychotherapy on immigrant clients seeking mental health services in Hawaii.
abstract: The present study sought to examine the effects of a standard role induction (role preparation) procedure on immigrant patients having their first therapy experience. Thirty immigrant clients who met selection criteria and were seeking treatment at a community mental health center in Hawaii were assigned to either role induction (therapy preparation intervention) or a placebo intervention prior to receiving therapy offered by 10 professional therapists. The effects of the role-induction or placebo manipulation were assessed by a measure of expectancy, satisfaction ratings, and data on premature termination and attendance. Results indicated that the patients who received the role preparation procedure as well as placebo patients had changed their expectations in appropriate ways by the end of therapy. The role-prepared patients, however, became less dependent on their therapist for support, advice, and direction. In addition, the role-prepared patients were more satisfied with therapy, rated themselves as more changed, and dropped out of treatment at significantly lower rates. The implications of the results for service delivery to immigrant patients were examined.

screening.rationale: Empirical trial tested causal effects of a role-preparation psychosocial manipulation versus a placebo intervention on expectancy, satisfaction, and dropout, meeting inclusion for placebo/context effects.

classification.summary: Tested role-preparation versus a placebo intervention in 30 immigrant clients and found role-prepared patients had greater satisfaction, self-rated change, lower dropout, and less dependency on therapists.
classification.key_finding: Role-prepared patients reported greater satisfaction and lower premature termination than placebo-intervention patients (N=30).

title: Demand effects for desensitization and two placebos in a dental fear context.
journal: Journal of behavior therapy and experimental psychiatry
abstract: Forty-five subjects sampled two sessions of a prototype desensitization treatment, two sessions of the Modified Avoidance Response Placebo or two sessions of Pseudotherapy. Each subject simulated the effects on dental fear of the experimental regimen to which he was exposed. Each subject also rated the credibility of the sampled regimen. Both the simulation data and the credibility ratings showed the Modified Avoidance Response Placebo to be the preferred control for "nonspecifics" in dental-fear desensitization experiments.

screening.rationale: Empirical study that experimentally compared two placebo controls and assessed credibility/demand effects in a dental-fear desensitization context, focusing on placebo control suitability (methodology of placebo science).

classification.summary: Compared two placebo controls and a desensitization regimen in 45 volunteers and found the Modified Avoidance Response Placebo rated as the more credible control for nonspecific effects in dental-fear desensitization experiments.
classification.key_finding: Participants rated the Modified Avoidance Response Placebo as more credible/preferred for controlling nonspecifics than the Pseudotherapy placebo.

title: Adverse reactions to triazolam, flurazepam, and placebo in controlled clinical trials.
abstract: Adverse reactions were evaluated from 45 double-blind controlled clinical trials involving triazolam 0.25 mg (N = 731), triazolam 0.5 mg (N = 2004), flurazepam 30 mg (N = 899), and placebo (N = 1771). Excessive CNS depression was the most frequent adverse effect, reported in 14.2% of trials with triazolam 0.25 mg, 19.5% with triazolam 0.5 mg, 23.9% with flurazepam 30 mg, and 6.4% with placebo. With the exception of orolingual complaints associated with flurazepam, all other categories of adverse reactions were equally or more frequent with placebo than with active medications. Unusual or excessive adverse reactions were not reported.

screening.rationale: Quantitative synthesis of adverse reactions across trials explicitly compared placebo adverse-event rates versus active drugs, making placebo/nocebo responses the object of analysis.

classification.summary: Pooled adverse-reaction data from 45 double-blind trials of triazolam, flurazepam, and placebo and found many adverse-event categories were equally or more frequent with placebo, while excessive CNS depression was more common with active drugs.
classification.key_finding: Placebo showed substantial adverse-event reporting (e.g., 6.4% excessive CNS depression) and several adverse categories were as frequent or more frequent on placebo than on active benzodiazepines.

title: Alcohol, aggression and assertiveness in men: dosage and expectancy effects.
abstract: The effect of alcohol on aggression and assertiveness was examined in 54 men college students. A 2 (high vs low dosage expectancy) x 3 (0.0, 0.5 and 1.0 ml of 95% alcohol per kg of body weight) design was used. There was an increase in self-reported aggression at the moderate dosage but an increase only in profanity at the high dosage. The expectancy manipulation also produced an increase in self-reported aggression. Actual dosage and dosage expectancy did not influence assertiveness.

screening.rationale: Experimental manipulation of alcohol dosage and dosage-expectancy examined expectancy (context) effects on aggression, an active-drug context manipulation meeting inclusion criteria for placebo/expectation effects.

classification.summary: Tested alcohol dose and dosage-expectancy in 54 college men and found moderate dose and high expectancy increased self-reported aggression, while assertiveness was unaffected.
classification.key_finding: Moderate alcohol dose increased self-reported aggression and expectancy manipulation increased self-reported aggression; no effects on assertiveness (N=54).

title: Placebo application, personality, and headaches: a signal detection theory analysis of experimentally induced pain in comparison to clinical pain.
abstract: 45 patients suffering from severe chronic intermittent headaches were divided into 3 groups matched for sex, and assigned to a double-blind 5-week cross-over design with 3 X 1 g/d metamizole--a mild analgesic of the pyrazolone type--a placebo, or a no-treatment control condition. For each of the 6 sessions (t0-t5) signal detection theory parameters d' and log beta for assessment of electrical pain perception and headache ratings on the preceding treatment period were obtained. At t0 all patients were examined via a personality inventory. There were no significant drug effects on headache and signal detection theory parameters, but a clear decrease of the discrimination index d' and of clinical pain over time, regardless of the mode of treatment. No relationship between pathological and experimentally induced pain could be demonstrated. There was no significant negative correlation between response bias of judgement of stimulus intensity (log beta) and neuroticism.

screening.rationale: Double-blind crossover trial with placebo and no-treatment arms allowed estimation of placebo effects/responses and analyzed personality moderators.

classification.summary: Randomized double-blind crossover trial in 45 chronic headache patients compared metamizole, placebo, and no-treatment and found decreases in discrimination index and clinical pain over time regardless of treatment.
classification.key_finding: Found no drug-specific effects and no placebo-specific benefit versus no-treatment; clinical pain and experimental discrimination decreased over time across all conditions.

title: Role of loperamide and placebo in management of irritable bowel syndrome (IBS).
abstract: Symptom scores, stool data, and the transit of a standard, solid meal were measured in 28 patients with irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) during baseline conditions and after five weeks of treatment with placebo and loperamide, given as a flexible dosage regime in the form of a double-blind, cross-over trial. All patients had undergone a comprehensive series of diagnostic investigations and had failed to respond to dietary supplementation with coarse wheat bran (10-30 g daily). Loperamide treatment accelerated gastric emptying, compared with placebo (1.2 +/- 0.1 vs 1.5 +/- 0.1 hr; P less than 0.001) and delayed both small bowel (6.2 +/- 0.3 vs 4.3 +/- 0.3 hr; P less than 0.001) and whole gut transit (56 +/- 5 vs 42 +/- 4 hr; P less than 0.01). Eighteen patients said they felt better taking loperamide compared with placebo and, at follow up, 15 of these patients remained satisfied with the effects of the drug. Most symptoms improved significantly on placebo compared with the baseline period, but three of these [diarrhea (P less than 0.01), urgency (P less than 0.01) and borborygmi (P less than 0.05)] showed a further significant improvement on loperamide. Improvement in diarrhea was not associated with any change in stool weight but was associated with reductions in stool frequency (P less than 0.001), passage of unformed stools (P less than 0.01), and incidence of urgency (P less than 0.001). Urgency was the only symptom that was significantly more common in the success group, compared with the group who did not feel better on loperamide.

screening.rationale: The randomized double-blind crossover trial reported and analyzed symptomatic improvement during the placebo period (placebo response) in IBS, meeting inclusion criteria for placebo response studies.

classification.summary: Found that most IBS symptoms improved significantly during the placebo period versus baseline, while loperamide produced additional symptomatic and objective effects on gut transit.
classification.key_finding: Most symptoms improved on placebo versus baseline; loperamide further improved diarrhea, urgency, and borborygmi and altered gastric emptying, small-bowel, and whole-gut transit.

title: Heart rate biofeedback and cold pressor pain: effects of expectancy.
abstract: The study investigated the effects of expectancy on the reduction of cold pressor test pain using heart rate biofeedback training. Thirty-six male subjects were given an initial 45-sec cold pressor test, 25 heart rate decrease feedback training trials, and a final cold pressor test in which they were told to decrease their heart rate, but without the aid of feedback. Two levels of outcome expectancy (increase pain, decrease pain) and two levels of cold pressor water temperature (0 degrees C, 5 degrees C), resulting in four groups (N = 9 per group), were used to assess the interaction between expectancy and aversive stimulus intensity. Immediately prior to the final cold pressor test, the increase pain expectancy subjects were told that decreasing their heart rate during the ice water immersion would cause more pain. Decrease pain subjects were told that decreasing their heart rate would cause less pain. Expectancy was found to be the major determinant of pain reports. The decrease pain subjects consistently reported less pain on the final cold pressor, whereas the increase pain subjects consistently reported more pain. Contrary to prediction, expectancy effects were greater for the colder water. The findings indicate the importance of expectancy in the clinical use of biofeedback to control pain.

screening.rationale: Experimental human study that manipulated outcome expectancy and measured its causal effect on cold pressor pain reports.

classification.summary: Manipulated expectancies during heart-rate biofeedback training and found expectancy strongly determined cold pressor pain reports, with decrease-expectancy reducing pain and increase-expectancy increasing pain.
classification.key_finding: Expectancy direction reliably altered pain ratings: decrease-expectancy reduced reported pain while increase-expectancy increased it; effects were larger at colder temperature.

title: Duration of antidepressant drug treatment. What is an adequate trial?
abstract: Data from three six-week placebo-controlled randomized antidepressant trials were pooled to test the hypothesis that a four-week trial is insufficient to reach a determination of drug failure in depressed patients. We compared global clinical ratings at weekly intervals for patients receiving drug and patients receiving placebo and calculated the proportion of patients whose clinical status changed over time. We predicted, and found, that a significant proportion of patients who showed no clear-cut response at four weeks would show much improvement at six weeks in drug but not placebo conditions. Baseline Research Diagnostic Criteria diagnosis, baseline illness severity, and drug dose adjustments after four weeks did not predict either late clinical improvement or relapse between four and six weeks. Additional placebo-controlled studies are needed to replicate our findings concerning the advantage of extending trials to five or six weeks in samples of patients of various depressive subtypes.
mesh: Outcome and Process Assessment, Health Care

screening.rationale: Pooled analysis of three placebo-controlled RCTs that explicitly compared weekly clinical ratings in drug versus placebo to assess time-course and placebo arm stability, addressing placebo response and trial duration methodology.

classification.summary: Pooled data from three six-week antidepressant RCTs compared weekly clinical ratings and found many drug nonresponders at four weeks improved by six weeks, whereas placebo patients did not show similar late improvement.
classification.key_finding: Found that a substantial proportion of patients who had not responded by week 4 showed clear improvement by week 6 on active drug but not on placebo, supporting extending trials to five–six weeks.

title: Cranial electrotherapy stimulation treatment of cognitive brain dysfunction in chemical dependence.
abstract: Several studies have shown that cranial electrotherapy stimulation (CES) is useful in treating brain dysfunction associated with alcoholism. A double-blind study replicated the latest of these findings in 60 inpatients and extended them by treating individuals with alcoholism and other chemical dependencies. Treatment effects were assessed on three subscales of the WAIS that are clinical indicators of organic brain syndrome. No placebo effect was found. CES appears to be a valuable adjunct to rehabilitation programs for addicted persons and can effect changes in areas not addressed by other treatment modalities.

screening.rationale: Double-blind randomized trial of cranial electrotherapy with a sham device control that reported on placebo effects (stated 'No placebo effect was found'), so placebo/sham response is an object of study.

classification.summary: Randomized double-blind trial (N=60) tested cranial electrotherapy stimulation vs sham in inpatients with alcoholism/chemical dependence and found CES improved WAIS subscales while no placebo (sham) effect was observed.
classification.key_finding: No placebo (sham) effect on WAIS subscales; active CES produced measurable cognitive improvements.

title: In search of a status for acupuncture.
journal: South African medical journal = Suid-Afrikaanse tydskrif vir geneeskunde
abstract: Acupuncture treatment is currently generating increased interest in various parts of the world. The effectiveness of this quasi-medical procedure, which has survived for almost 5 000 years, is considered on the strength of statistical data obtained at an institution where such treatment is applied under acceptable scientific circumstances. Explanations are sought for the encompassing extent of treatment claims and the continued support for this technique which is often subjected to severe criticism in modern contexts. The roles of literacy, tradition and convention, a placebo effect and psychological factors as explanatory agents are discussed. The procedure also has possible psychophysical and physiological foundations which sufficiently warrant further scientific effort to find an explanation for this phenomenon.

screening.rationale: Paper reviewed acupuncture effectiveness and explicitly discussed the placebo effect and psychological/contextual explanations as central explanatory agents, meeting the 'placebo science' inclusion criterion.

classification.summary: Discussed the effectiveness of acupuncture and considered placebo, psychological, cultural, and possible physiological explanations, concluding that further scientific study was warranted.

title: Are there two studies that clearly reveal superiority of drug over placebo?

screening.rationale: No abstract or full text available; title suggests a methodological/commentary piece about trials comparing drug and placebo but insufficient information to determine whether placebo effects/responses are analyzed as an object of study.

classification.summary: Discusses whether two studies clearly demonstrate drug superiority over placebo, focusing on clinical trial design and statistical interpretation.

title: Placebos: who's being fooled?

screening.rationale: No abstract or full text provided; title suggests a discussion of placebo prescribing/ethics but insufficient information to confirm whether placebo/nocebo is a primary subject or an empirical study.

classification.summary: No abstract available; title implies a discussion about who is deceived by placebos, likely addressing placebo prescribing or ethics in pharmacy, but content and aims are unclear.

title: Premedication with flunitrazepam, diazepam and placebo in the apprehensive child.
journal: ASDC journal of dentistry for children

screening.rationale: Title indicates a double-blind comparative trial including a placebo arm for premedication in apprehensive children, but absence of abstract/full-text prevents judging whether placebo/nocebo effects or placebo-arm responses were analyzed versus serving solely as a control for drug efficacy.

classification.summary: No abstract available; reported a double-blind comparative study of flunitrazepam, diazepam, and placebo as premedication in apprehensive children undergoing dental care.

title: Placebos: how much do you know about them?

screening.rationale: No abstract or full text available to determine whether the article empirically studied placebo/nocebo effects or was a survey/commentary about placebo knowledge/ethics.

classification.summary: Likely discussed nurses' knowledge and ethical issues regarding placebos, but no abstract or full text was available to confirm methods or findings.

title: Functional structure of the placebo response.

screening.rationale: Title and MeSH terms explicitly name placebo/placebo response and psychophysiological measures in humans, indicating the paper's primary focus on placebo response.

classification.summary: Studied the functional structure of the placebo response in adult humans, focusing on blood pressure, pulse, emotions, and motor activity.

title: Placebos, patients, and physicians.
journal: The Pharos of Alpha Omega Alpha-Honor Medical Society. Alpha Omega Alpha
journal_abbrev: Pharos Alpha Omega Alpha Honor Med Soc

screening.rationale: MeSH terms indicate the article addresses attitudes/ethics of physicians and patients about placebos, which meets inclusion for placebo science (surveys/attitudes).

classification.summary: Reported on physicians' and patients' attitudes and ethical issues concerning placebo use.

title: The haemodynamic effects of labetalol, ketanserin and a placebo at the end of a NLA. A double blind study.

screening.rationale: No abstract or full text available; title shows a placebo comparator in a double-blind drug trial but provides no information whether placebo/nocebo effects or responses were analyzed as the study aim.

classification.summary: Insufficient information in the record to determine whether the study analyzed placebo/nocebo effects; reported as a double-blind comparison of labetalol, ketanserin, and placebo on hemodynamics.

title: Treatment of IUD related menorrhagia by indomethacin.
abstract: Indomethacin, prostaglandin synthetase inhibitor was tested in 9 women wearing a lippes loop IUD. These women suffered from excessive bleeding with a mean menstrual blood loss of more than 100 ml. The effect was studied by quantifying menstrual blood loss in a double blind 4 periods crossover study. The mean percentage reduction during treatment was of 57 percent. No significant placebo effect was observed. The effect of indomethacin support the contention that IUD's associated menorrhagia, is connected to an abnormal prostaglandin synthetase in the endometrium.

screening.rationale: Randomized double-blind crossover trial included a placebo condition and explicitly reported analysis of placebo effect (no significant placebo effect), so placebo/placebo-response is an object of study.

classification.summary: Conducted a double-blind four-period crossover trial in nine women with Lippes loop IUD menorrhagia and found indomethacin reduced menstrual blood loss by 57% while no significant placebo effect was observed.
classification.key_finding: Indomethacin produced a mean 57% reduction in menstrual blood loss; placebo produced no significant change.

title: An eighteenth century view of the placebo effect (Rétif de la Bretonne).
abstract: Placebo - the promise to please the Lord of medieval prayer became the "pious fraud" (Thomas Jefferson) of late 18th century medical practice. Quoted here is Rétif de la Bretonne (1734-1806), one of the most prolific novelists and popular encyclopedists ever, also highly regarded by some illustrious critics, as he is giving his cynical views about the "prejudices", (rather then "placebos") in religion, politics, and the art of healing.

screening.rationale: Historical analysis focusing on the concept and history of 'placebo' qualifies as placebo science broadly (history/conceptual work).

classification.summary: Reviews eighteenth-century perspectives on placebo and the notion of 'pious fraud' through writings of Rétif de la Bretonne.

title: Hip joint distension in osteoarthrosis. A triple-blind controlled study comparing the effect of intra-articular indoprofen with placebo.
abstract: In a triple-blind controlled study, significant pain alleviation (p less than 0.01) was registered in patients with osteoarthrosis (OA) of the hip in the first 24 h after hip joint distension. There was no significant difference between treatment with indoprofen (a new non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug for intra-articular use) and placebo. Pain relief lasted for at least 12 weeks in approximately half of the patients, in whom a significant increase in joint mobility was registered. Intra-articular indoprofen was not superior to placebo as regards pain relief or increased joint mobility. These findings indicate that the effect of a single hip joint distension in OA is due to a mechanical distension of the joint capsule, perhaps involving disruption of local agglutinations, and not due to suppression of inflammation.

screening.rationale: Although a drug efficacy RCT, the paper analyzed and reported the within-arm pain relief after intra-articular injection and concluded the effect was due to mechanical joint distension (i.e., placebo/sham response was analyzed and interpreted).

classification.summary: Conducted a triple-blind RCT comparing intra-articular indoprofen versus placebo for hip OA and found significant pain relief and increased joint mobility after joint distension in both groups, with no superiority of indoprofen.
classification.key_finding: Pain relief in the first 24 h (p < 0.01) occurred after joint distension in both drug and placebo groups, with no significant difference between them.

title: Surgical trial: possibilities and objections.
journal: European surgical research. Europaische chirurgische Forschung. Recherches chirurgicales europeennes
abstract: Trials are widely regarded as the best method for assessing the effectiveness of new techniques. The placebo effect of surgery is a real but little considered fact; other problems that arise in surgical trials are the skills of the participating surgeons, the random assignment of patients and the impossibility of a wholly blind approach. This paper discusses these matters.

screening.rationale: Included because the paper's main subject is the placebo effect and methodological challenges of surgical trials (placebo science / trial methodology).

classification.summary: Discusses the reality of surgical placebo effects and methodological challenges in surgical trials, including blinding, surgeon skill, and randomization.

title: A comparative study of the pain alleviating effect of vibratory stimulation, transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation, electroacupuncture and placebo.
journal: The American journal of Chinese medicine
abstract: The pain reducing effect of vibratory stimulation at 100 Hz, transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS) at 100 Hz, electroacupuncture at 2 Hz as compared to placebo was studied in 36 patients suffering from myalgia. In 29 patients these modes of stimulation produced pain reduction. Out of these patients 18 rated vibratory stimulation, TENS or electroacupuncture as more effective than placebo while 6 patients rated placebo as more effective. Five patients rated the pain suppressive effect of vibratory stimulation, TENS and electroacupuncture as being equal to that of placebo. Four of the patients who experienced pain reduction with peripheral stimulation reported an effect only for one particular type of peripheral stimulation. The present results provide evidence that vibratory stimulation, TENS and electroacupuncture are as efficient pain suppressive measures and superior to placebo. It is suggested on the basis of these findings that vibratory stimulation, TENS and electroacupuncture merit consideration in the choice of treatment of myalgia.

screening.rationale: Randomized comparative trial directly compared peripheral stimulation modalities against a placebo control and reported placebo-relative effects on pain.

classification.summary: Found that vibratory stimulation, TENS, and electroacupuncture produced pain reduction in most myalgia patients and were generally superior to placebo.
classification.key_finding: In 29/36 patients stimulation reduced pain; 18 rated active stimulation as more effective than placebo while 6 rated placebo better.

title: Placebo effects in biofeedback and self-perception of muscle tension.

screening.rationale: Title explicitly addresses placebo effects in biofeedback and self-perception of muscle tension, indicating placebo was the object of study despite no abstract.

classification.summary: Studied placebo effects in biofeedback and self-perception of muscle tension in human participants, focusing on subjective perception and biofeedback signals.

title: Information, compliance and side-effects: a study of patients on antidepressant medication.
abstract: A study was carried out to elucidate whether the improved compliance associated with the provision of verbal and written information about a prescribed drug is due to the specific information or to a non-specific attention-placebo effect. 120 depressed outpatients were prescribed dothiepin and randomly allocated to one of three groups: Group A were given verbal and written information about side-effects; Group B were given verbal and written information about beneficial effects; Group C were told only that the drug was being given to treat their depression and received no written information. Compliance with medication was assessed at 3 weeks and 6 weeks by interrogation and by pill count. At the same time, side-effects were enquired for and their occurrence or non-occurrence noted. No significant differences were found between the groups in the rates of compliance at either 3 weeks or 6 weeks. When Groups A and B were combined to give a total 'information' group and compared with Group C--the 'no-information' group--the rate of compliance at 3 weeks was significantly higher (P less than 0.05) in the 'information' group. No significant differences were found between the groups in the rates of reported side-effects at either 3 weeks or 6 weeks. When Groups A and C were combined and compared with Group B (information about beneficial effects), side-effects were found to be reported significantly less frequently (P less than 0.05) in the latter at 6 weeks. Of 175 compliance estimates, 97.7% gave concordant results for estimation by interrogation and by pill count.(ABSTRACT TRUNCATED AT 250 WORDS)

screening.rationale: Randomized trial manipulated verbal/written information to test whether information/attention influenced compliance and side-effect reporting (placebo/nocebo context effects).

classification.summary: Randomized depressed outpatients received different verbal/written information about dothiepin; information increased 3-week compliance and benefit-focused information reduced reported side-effects at 6 weeks.
classification.key_finding: Information (verbal/written) increased compliance at 3 weeks (p<0.05) and information about benefits led to fewer reported side-effects at 6 weeks (p<0.05).

title: Influence of the method of drug administration on analgesic response.
abstract: The appropriate control group in studies of placebo-induced analgesia has not been established. A traditional control has been a 'no treatment' or natural-history group. In some studies, the natural-history group receives a hidden infusion of vehicle, a physiologically inactive substance such as saline solution, to eliminate differences in expectation of the outcome on the part of the experimenter. To evaluate whether 'hidden' as well as open infusion of vehicle can elicit a placebo response, we have now tested a different natural-history group, one which received an infusion of vehicle from a syringe pump controlled by a programmable timer. A comparison of these two control groups provides evidence that hidden infusion of vehicle can elicit a placebo response. Use of this new control group also permitted a clear distinction between a naloxone-antagonizable component of placebo analgesia and naloxone antagonism of endorphin-mediated analgesia induced by surgical stress. Our study underscores the power of the placebo and emphasizes that even the most subtle cues can elicit a placebo response.

screening.rationale: Empirical human study that directly manipulated method of administration (open vs hidden infusion) to test causal placebo analgesia and its naloxone-sensitive mechanism.

classification.summary: Compared open versus hidden vehicle infusions and found that hidden (automated) infusion elicited placebo analgesia, part of which was antagonized by naloxone, implicating endogenous opioids.
classification.key_finding: Hidden infusion produced measurable placebo analgesia that was naloxone-antagonizable, suggesting an opioid-mediated component.

title: The placebo. Conceptual analysis of a construct in transition.
mesh: Outcome and Process Assessment, Health Care

screening.rationale: Title indicates a conceptual/theoretical analysis of the placebo construct, which meets inclusion for placebo science broadly despite no abstract.

classification.summary: Provided a conceptual analysis of the placebo as a changing construct and discussed its implications for psychotherapy and healthcare practice.

title: Prostaglandin synthetase inhibitors in the treatment of primary dysmenorrhea. Outcome trials reviewed.
journal: American journal of obstetrics and gynecology
abstract: Clinical trials of prostaglandin synthetase inhibitors (PGSIs) prescribed for the treatment of primary dysmenorrhea were reviewed as to pain relief effectiveness, frequency and nature of side effects, and methodological adequacy. The review investigated 51 PGSI trials for a total of 1,649 women and 682 menstrual cycles and found that, over all, 72% of dysmenorrheic women reported significant pain relief to PGSI, 18% reported minimal or no pain relief, and 15% showed placebo response. Comparisons among the fenamatic compounds, ibuprofen, indomethacin, and naproxen showed the fenamates to be more effective in providing pain relief. PGSI-associated side effects were minimal for all PGSIs with the exception of indomethacin. Results were evaluated with respect to several methodological problems. Conclusions were drawn that despite these shortcomings, PGSIs are undoubtedly effective and safe for the majority of women with primary dysmenorrhea.

screening.rationale: Reviewed 51 clinical trials and reported a pooled placebo response rate (15%) and methodological issues, so placebo response and trial methodology were substantive objects of study.

classification.summary: Reviewed 51 trials of prostaglandin synthetase inhibitors for primary dysmenorrhea and reported treatment effectiveness, side effects, methodological concerns, and a pooled placebo response of about 15%.
classification.key_finding: Found that across 51 trials (1,649 women) ~15% showed a placebo response and PGSIs were generally effective.

title: A new device for administering placebo alcohol.
abstract: Placebo alcohol administered via a new device induced intoxication in 7 of 10 healthy adult males. Intoxication levels reported after placebo alcohol was 36% of intoxication ratings after real alcohol when peak blood alcohol values reached 84 mg/dl. Since expectancy about alcohol effects may contribute significantly to perceived intoxication, the new device should facilitate alcohol administration studies which would benefit from a placebo control.

screening.rationale: Empirical human study whose stated aim and analysis concerned placebo alcohol administration and its subjective intoxication (placebo effect/response).

classification.summary: Tested a new device to administer placebo alcohol in healthy adult males and found 7/10 reported intoxication, with placebo ratings about 36% of real alcohol ratings.
classification.key_finding: Placebo alcohol produced subjective intoxication in 7 of 10 men, averaging 36% of the intoxication ratings seen with real alcohol.

title: The subtractive expectancy placebo procedure: a measure of non-specific factors in behavioural interventions.

screening.rationale: Title indicates the paper proposed/measured a placebo/expectancy procedure to assess non-specific factors in behavioural interventions, meeting inclusion for placebo science/methods.

classification.summary: Described the 'subtractive expectancy placebo' procedure as a method to measure non-specific (placebo/expectancy) factors in behavioral interventions.

title: The analgesic effects of transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation and placebo in chronic pain patients. A double-blind non-crossover comparison.
abstract: The analgesic effects of high frequency transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TNS), "acupuncture-like" TNS and placebo TNS were evaluated in 33 patients with rheumatoid arthritis and chronic hand pain using a randomized, double-blind, non-crossover design. An oscilloscope was employed to monitor the stimulator output in the TNS treatment groups and to provide strong suggestion and a focus of attention in the placebo treatment group. The two forms of TNS were applied at the highest intensity that could be tolerated by patients. Assessments of resting pain, joint tenderness, grip strength and grip pain were made before and after treatment. The pain and joint tenderness measurements showed high frequency TNS, "acupuncture-like" TNS and placebo TNS to be equally effective in producing analgesia of similar degree and trend over time. The grip strength measurements showed no significant change. The results obtained with placebo are probably due to the suggestion and attention effects of the visual stimulus. The implications of these results in respect to pain control pathways are discussed. Although TNS given at high intensity was shown to be no better than placebo applied with strong suggestion, this does not preclude its use as a method of pain control in rheumatoid arthritis.

screening.rationale: Randomized double-blind trial that compared active TNS to placebo TNS and analyzed the placebo response/effect (placebo produced comparable analgesia), meeting inclusion criteria for placebo effect research.

classification.summary: Found that high-frequency and acupuncture-like TNS and placebo TNS produced similar reductions in resting pain and joint tenderness in 33 rheumatoid arthritis patients, while grip strength did not change.
classification.key_finding: Placebo TNS with strong suggestion produced analgesia comparable to active TNS in subjective and tenderness measures.

title: The persistence of stimulant effects in chronically treated children: further evidence of an inverse relationship between drug effects and placebo levels of response.
abstract: Seventeen hyperactive children who had been treated for 1-5 years with methylphenidate were studied in a double-blind placebo-controlled crossover study. Specific measures of stimulant response were found to be inversely related to the subject's level of response in the placebo condition. This inverse relationship was previously found to characterize the clinical effects of hyperactive children in an acute-treatment paradigm. It is equally valid in a chronic-treatment study. "State-contingency" is not, therefore, simply a function of the "novelty" of initial drug treatment.

screening.rationale: Double-blind placebo-controlled crossover trial that analyzed placebo-condition levels and their inverse relationship with stimulant drug effects, making placebo response/effect the object of study.

classification.summary: Studied 17 chronically treated hyperactive children in a double-blind placebo-controlled crossover and found an inverse relationship between stimulant drug effects and levels of response in the placebo condition.
classification.key_finding: Found that higher placebo-condition response predicted smaller stimulant treatment effects (inverse relationship).
